Thanks for raising that concern. I agree that introducing different
behavior based on fallback={null} versus fallback={undefined} or an omitted
fallback could make Suspense semantics harder to reason about and
potentially introduce edge cases.

The comparison with use() is interesting. One thing I noticed while
investigating is that React.lazy currently initializes its payload only
when first rendered, and when it receives an already-resolved native
Promise it still has to go through a microtask before the payload state can
transition from pending. That seems to put it on a different path from
resources consumed through use().

If the underlying issue is that React.lazy cannot synchronously observe
fulfillment of an already-resolved Promise, then improving convergence
between the use() and React.lazy implementations may be a cleaner long-term
direction than adding fallback-specific throttling exceptions. It would
avoid creating special cases in Suspense behavior while potentially
addressing the extra delay more generally.

I'm curious whether maintainers view the current behavior as an intentional
consequence of React.lazy initialization semantics, or whether alignment
with the mechanisms used by use() is something worth exploring.

On Fri, Jun 19, 2026, 4:05 PM MaxwellCohen ***@***.***> wrote:

> *MaxwellCohen* left a comment (react/react#36569)
> <https://github.com/react/react/issues/36569#issuecomment-4754699834>
>
> I think this is an issue with Rect.lazy internal implementation compared
> to use implementation is diffrent. When use has a resolved promise the
> first time, Suspense does not wait 300ms to see the console logs in this
> sandbox <https://codesandbox.io/p/sandbox/dcjmsz>.
>
> I wonder if there is a way to combine the internal implementations of use
> and Rect.lazy to leverage subclass promises, allowing React to read the
> value synchronously without waiting on a microtask and reducing some
> simi-duplicative code.
>
> Special casing <Suspense fallback={null}> vs <Suspense
> fallback={undefined}> or <Suspense> seems like something that would be
> hard to learn or create bugs.
